rows.text: I’d say I’m moderately likely—maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10—because $99/month is actually doable compared to the $349 branded meds and I like that it’s focused on ApoB and blood pressure, which I’m genuinely worried about. My hesitation is I don’t want to pay for “tracking” if there’s no real plan to lower it, and I’d need to know if they can prescribe anything or coordinate meds, not just tell me to eat better. Also, coronary calcium scoring usually costs extra, so I’d want to know what’s included versus what I’d get billed for separately.

I’d be pretty interested—maybe a 7/10 likely—because heart stuff feels very real for me with my dad and my brother, and I like that it’s a real physician and not some “wellness” coaching thing. The $99/month gives me pause though; even with decent insurance, I’m used to care being covered and I’d want to know what’s included (labs, calcium scan cost, meds) before I commit. I also worry it could turn into an endless subscription unless there’s a clear plan and timeline for what “success” looks like and when I could reasonably stop.

I’d say moderately likely—maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10—because my calcium score is 280 and my PCP basically shrugged and offered a statin with no real plan, and I’m tired of 10–12 minute visits. $99/month is not crazy if it truly includes tight follow-up on ApoB/BP and someone who’ll adjust meds and make a concrete strategy, and I can use my HSA. My hesitation is whether this is actual medical management (ordering labs, prescribing, handling side effects, coordinating imaging) or more of a “coaching” subscription that still dumps the hard stuff back on me, and whether they’ll just push a statin and call it a day.

I’d say I’m moderately likely—probably like a 6 or 7 out of 10—because $99/month is doable for me compared to the $349 branded meds, and I’m genuinely worried about my blood pressure and heart risk if I regain weight. My hesitation is it sounds more like monitoring and coaching than actually providing the medication support that helped me lose 48 pounds, so I’d need to know what “works with you” really means. I’d also want clarity on what testing costs extra (ApoB labs, coronary calcium scan) and whether they can coordinate meds if I need something, otherwise it could turn into another expensive add-on.

I’d be pretty interested—maybe a 7/10—because with my dad and brother, the “actually lower it” part and having a real physician monitoring ApoB and blood pressure feels more legitimate than the usual wellness stuff. My hesitation is the $99/month on top of everything else; I’d want to know exactly what’s included (labs, calcium scan, meds, follow-ups) because those can add up fast. I also already have decent insurance through the district, so I’d need a clear reason why this is better than just seeing my primary care or a cardiologist. If I could use my HSA and it wasn’t a hard sell or gimmicky, I’d seriously consider trying it for a few months.

I’d say I’m moderately likely—maybe a 7/10—because after getting a 280 calcium score and basically a shrug + “here’s a statin,” I’m pretty motivated to have someone actually track ApoB/BP and give me a plan. The $99/month is reasonable and I can use my HSA, but I’d hesitate until I know exactly what “works with you” means (meds like statins/ezetimibe/PCSK9, BP meds, follow-up cadence, lab costs, and whether they’ll order/interpret scans). I’d also want to be sure it’s not just generic lifestyle coaching and that the doctor will coordinate with my PCP and provide clear targets and timelines, not more vague “keep an eye on it.”

I’d say I’m moderately likely, maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10, mostly because my dad died of a heart attack at 58 and my brother just had a stent, so this hits close to home. I like that it’s a real physician tracking concrete numbers (ApoB, blood pressure, calcium score) and not some “wellness” program, but I’d want to know what’s actually included—like do they order the tests, what do those tests cost, and do they prescribe meds if needed. $99/month is doable but not nothing on a teacher budget, so if the labs and scans are extra and expensive, I’d hesitate or try to do it through my regular doctor/insurance first. Cancel anytime and HSA-eligible helps, but I’d need reassurance it’s not just messaging and generic advice.

I’m somewhat likely, maybe a 6–7/10, mostly because my calcium score is 280 and my PCP basically shrugged and tossed me a statin with no plan, which drives me nuts. If this is truly a physician who will set targets (ApoB, BP) and track progress with actual follow-up, I’d pay $99/month out of my HSA without blinking for at least a few months.

My hesitations are: what “bring them down” really means (you can’t exactly reverse CAC reliably), whether they’ll just push supplements and generic advice, and whether they’ll coordinate labs/imaging locally without me getting surprise costs. I’d want to see exactly what’s included—frequency of visits, lab ordering, medication management, and whether they’ll use evidence-based thresholds for ApoB and actually adjust treatment instead of just “keep an eye on it.”

I’d say I’m moderately likely—maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10—because $99/month feels doable compared to what I’m staring at for the branded meds, and I like that it’s focused on real numbers like blood pressure and ApoB. My hesitation is it doesn’t sound like it includes anything to help me stay on semaglutide or a weight-loss medication plan, and that’s my biggest fear right now because I don’t want the weight and blood pressure to creep back up. Also, the coronary calcium score part makes me wonder if that’s an extra cost and how much testing I’d end up paying for out of pocket.

I’m kind of on the fence—maybe a 5 or 6 out of 10. I like that it’s no insurance and “cancel anytime,” and the heart-risk angle hits home since I know my blood pressure’s been high and my wife’s been on me to get checked. But $99/month is a lot with my income bouncing around, and I’m skeptical it’ll turn into more tests and upsells—plus I don’t even know what ApoB is or how much the calcium scan costs on top of that. If they were really upfront about total costs and what I’d actually get each month, I’d be more likely.

I’m kind of on the fence, but I’d say maybe a 5 or 6 out of 10 I’d sign up. I like the “no insurance” part and having someone actually track numbers like blood pressure and heart stuff, because I know mine’s probably not great, and my wife’s been on me about it. But $99 a month adds up when work’s slow, and I’m skeptical it’s not just another subscription that tells you bad news and then tries to upsell labs or scans that cost a bunch more. If the calcium score and bloodwork are included or clearly priced, I’d be a lot more likely.

Probably not very likely, at least not right away. $99 a month feels like a lot on my budget, especially when I already pay for insurance even if the deductible is high. I like the idea of someone actually tracking things and messaging, but I’d need to know what I’m really getting for that price (like are the tests included—ApoB and that calcium scan—and are meds/refills handled), otherwise it sounds like another bill on top of what I’m already paying.

I’m moderately likely—maybe a 7/10—because it’s speaking directly to what I care about (ApoB optimization plus someone actually qualified to interpret results and act on them). The big hesitation is whether it’s truly physician-led and data-driven vs. generic “heart health coaching,” and how much of the plan is concrete (meds like statins/ezetimibe/PCSK9, BP protocols, follow-up cadence) versus vague lifestyle advice. Also, I already pay for Function and track a ton with Whoop, so I’d need to see clear differentiation and that they’ll integrate my existing labs and prioritize outcomes, not just education.

I’d say I’m maybe a 5 or 6 out of 10 likely. The idea of actually tracking stuff like blood pressure and getting a real plan sounds good, and I like “no insurance needed” and cancel anytime, but $99/month adds up fast when work is slow and I’m already wary of doctors pushing tests or meds. Also the coronary calcium scan and all that—am I paying extra for those, and where do I even go to get it done around here? If my wife kept on me and they were straight about total costs and didn’t treat me like a number, I could see trying it for a couple months.

I’d be pretty likely—maybe a 7/10—because it’s explicitly ApoB + BP + CAC with a board-certified physician, and I’m already paying for labs and tracking data anyway. The hesitations are: what kind of physician (cardiology/preventive lipidology vs generic “board-certified”), how aggressive they’ll be on ApoB targets (I’m aiming pretty low), and whether they’ll actually interpret my Function/Whoop data without turning it into dumbed-down coaching. Also, I’d want to know if CAC is included or if I’m paying $99/mo plus separate scan/labs, because if it’s mostly messaging on top of stuff I’m already doing, I might pass.

I’m moderately likely—maybe a 6–7/10—because “board-certified physician” + ApoB + CAC is exactly the lane I care about, and $99/month isn’t crazy if the guidance is truly high-signal. My hesitation is I already have Function for labs and I can get CAC and BP elsewhere, so the value has to be the physician interpretation + a concrete plan that actually moves ApoB (meds, lifestyle, follow-up cadence) rather than generic heart-health coaching. I’d also want to know who the physician is (preventive cardiology/lipid expertise?), how often they’ll adjust treatment, and whether they’ll prescribe/manage statins/ezetimibe/PCSK9 if needed—otherwise it feels redundant.

Probably not very likely right away—$99 a month is a lot for me, especially with everything else going up. I do worry about my blood pressure and heart stuff, but I’m already paying for insurance, even if the deductible is huge, so I’d need to see that this really replaces other costs I’m already stuck paying (like visits, labs, meds). Also I don’t even know what ApoB is, and the coronary calcium scan sounds like it could be an extra expensive test, so I’d want to know what’s included and what I’d still have to pay out of pocket. If they could show me clear pricing on tests and that I’d actually get consistent help adjusting meds like my lisinopril without surprise bills, then I’d consider it.

Probably not very likely right away—$99 a month is a lot for me on top of my insurance, especially with a $7k deductible and everything else getting more expensive. I like the idea of having a real doctor actually track things and message with me, because I’m basically just on lisinopril from urgent care and don’t have a regular doctor, but I’d need to know what tests like ApoB and a coronary calcium score would cost me and whether they’re included. If it truly replaced other bills I’m already paying (urgent care visits, random labs, etc.) and helped me avoid bigger problems, I’d consider it, but as written it feels like another monthly subscription.

I’d be pretty interested because my dad died of a heart attack at 58 and my brother just had a stent, so the “baseline your numbers and manage them down” part hits home. But I’m cautious—$99/month adds up, and I’d want to know what I’m actually getting beyond what my regular doctor and decent insurance already cover. I’d probably sign up if it’s truly a board-certified physician (not a “coach”) and they can order labs, coordinate meds, and communicate with my PCP; otherwise it feels a little like a wellness subscription with a nicer headline.

I’d be pretty interested, probably like a 7/10, because my dad died of a heart attack at 58 and my brother just had a stent, so the “baseline and manage it down” idea hits home. That said, I’m skeptical of anything that starts to feel like a wellness subscription, and $99/month adds up fast even with decent insurance—I'd want to know exactly what I’m getting and whether they’ll coordinate with my regular doctor. I’d also need reassurance it’s truly a board-certified physician (not a “coach”) and that they can order labs and meds through insurance/HSA without it turning into a hassle.

I’d say moderately likely—maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10—because my calcium score came back 280 and my PCP basically shrugged and offered a statin with no real plan. The “baseline and manage down” plus video/text access is appealing if it means actual tracking (lipids, ApoB, Lp(a), BP, maybe repeat imaging) and not another 12‑minute drive-by. My hesitations are whether it’s just generic advice repackaged, whether the doctor will actually order labs and adjust meds aggressively, and if $99/month turns into me still paying out-of-pocket for everything else with my high deductible—even if I can use my HSA. If they could show a concrete protocol, what targets they use, and how often they follow up, I’d be a lot more likely to pull the trigger.

I’d be pretty interested, honestly—my dad died of a heart attack at 58 and my brother just had a stent, so this hits close to home. But I’d hesitate because $99/month adds up and I already have decent insurance; I’d want to know what I’m actually getting beyond what my primary care doctor could do (labs included or extra, meds handled, how often you meet, etc.). If it feels like a real medical program with clear outcomes and not a wellness-coaching thing, I could see myself signing up—maybe “somewhat likely,” like a 6–7 out of 10.

I’d say I’m moderately likely—maybe a 6 or 7 out of 10—because after getting a 280 calcium score and basically a shrug + “here’s a statin,” I’m pretty motivated to have someone actually manage this with a plan. ApoB, Lp(a), blood pressure, A1c, maybe imaging follow-up) and actual accountability? I’d be moderately likely—maybe a 6–7/10—because after getting a calcium score of 280 and basically a shrug plus “here’s a statin,” I’m clearly not getting a real plan in a 12‑minute PCP visit. The “baseline your numbers and manage them down” plus video/text access sounds like what I actually want, and $99/month is within reason and HSA‑eligible.

My hesitation is I’d need specifics: what numbers (LDL/ApoB, Lp(a), BP, A1c?), how often labs are checked, and what the follow‑up cadence looks like beyond generic lifestyle advice. I’d also want to know it’s not just pushing prescriptions and that they’ll coordinate with my PCP and handle things like statin intolerance or adding meds if targets aren’t met. Cancel anytime helps, but I’d probably want a clear first‑month plan and deliverables before I commit long term.

I’d be pretty likely to sign up, mainly because $99/month feels doable compared to the $349 branded meds, and I’m honestly scared of my blood pressure creeping back up if I regain weight. I like the idea of a physician actually tracking labs and adjusting a plan, not just generic advice, and the HSA-eligible part helps. My hesitation is whether “manages them down” is real without access to an affordable GLP-1 option—if it’s basically coaching and reminders, I’d probably cancel pretty fast.

I’m kind of on the fence. The message hits home because my blood pressure’s been high and my wife’s been on me, but $99 a month is a lot when work’s up and down and I don’t have insurance. I’d also want to know what I’m actually getting for that price (labs, meds, any extra fees) and whether it’s just some subscription where they push pills or send generic advice; if it felt legit and straightforward, I might try it for a month or two.
